summaries.Geography: The Sand Roads link West Africa to North Africa and the Mediterranean, with onward connections to the Indian Ocean. The Sahel is the transition from Sahara to savanna. The WHP reading describes a 3.5-million-square-mile desert from Nile to Atlantic as a navigable dry sea.
summaries.Goods: Environmental variation encouraged exchange: coastal cloth, glassware, weapons and books; Saharan copper and salt; savanna grains; forest yams and kola nuts. West African gold and scarce salt drove exchange. Traders also sought ivory and kola nuts and offered horses, cloth, tools and weapons. Enslaved people suffered forced movement and exploitation.
summaries.Caravans: Berber pastoralists guided caravans, rented camels and improved saddles. Camels had wide toes and could go ten days without water, carrying about 400 pounds across the Sahara or 1,200 over short distances. The WHP reading dates dromedary reintroduction to about 300 BCE after Stone Age extinction, while noting debate. Caravans followed wells and oases, traveled in cool months and times, and paid tribute for safety. Slides: hundreds of people, up to 5,000 camels, nights, 70 days, 15–20 miles daily. WHP: 5,000–10,000 camels in the thirteenth century, October–March, about 20 miles daily.
summaries.Empires: Trade wealth supported monarchies and city-states, including historical Ghana, Mali and Songhai, broadly 500–1600 in the slides. WHP gives Mali 1235–1670 and Songhai 1430–1591. Niger floodplains grew sorghum, millet and rice. Rulers controlled routes and merchant movement to protect southern gold mines. Cities traded and made beads, iron tools and cotton textiles. Enslaved women faced domestic and sexual exploitation. Enslaved men served as officials, craftsmen, miners and farm laborers.
summaries.Islam: The WHP reading calls Islam the most important factor in trade expansion after seventh-century Arab conquests. Berbers and urban merchants and rulers converted. Shared Arabic, values, records, legal codes and contracts supported communication and trust. Local religions remained important outside cities. The reading estimates as many as 9.3 million enslaved travelers in 800–1800 and distinguishes voluntary pilgrimage. Ibn Battuta admired Mali. Mansa Musa’s lavish 1320s hajj affected Egypt’s economy and gold myths encouraged Portuguese exploration. New sea lanes reduced desert routes’ global importance, but caravans continued into the early twentieth century.
summaries.Samarkand: Uzbekistan; Silk Roads junction linking East and West, Europe, Asia and Africa. Silk and luxury fabrics went to Europe and the Middle East. Spices included cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and pepper from the Far East and India, used for flavor, medicine and preservation. Merchant settlement brought wealth, urban growth and caravanserais. Scholars advanced astronomy, mathematics and literature. The passage associates Persian, Central Asian and Islamic fusion with Registan Square’s madrasas and mosques.
summaries.Timbuktu: Mali; edge of the Sahara, crossroads toward the Mediterranean and Middle East. Gold collection, refining and distribution; Saharan salt used for preservation and currency. Gold bought salt, textiles, horses, weapons, silk and spices. WHP says the city began as a caravanserai. Libraries and madrasas preserved theology, law, philosophy, literature and science. Islamic and local West African influences shaped Djinguereber and Sankore Mosques, palaces, tombs and houses. Scholars spread Islam, influencing governance, education and the arts.
summaries.Calicut: Also Kozhikode, on the Malabar Coast of Kerala, India. An Indian Ocean hub with Arab, Chinese, Persian and European merchants in the class passage. Pepper, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon served cooking, medicine and perfume. Cotton muslin and calico and luxury silk were traded. Connections through the Red Sea or Persian Gulf and Middle East joined the Silk Roads to Samarkand. The passage says Arab traders brought Islamic learning, mosques, madrasas and libraries and cites Mishkal Mosque and Hindu Tali Temple as architectural diversity.
summaries.Connections: All three cities linked commerce with urban growth and cultural and intellectual exchange. Samarkand’s inland junction, Timbuktu’s desert-edge crossroads and Calicut’s maritime coast shaped their connections and goods. Possible modern legacies are reasoned inferences from the reading’s architecture, libraries, manuscripts and cultural identities.
summaries.HIPPO: Class definition: Historical Context, Intended Audience, Purpose, Point of View, Organization. Ask where and when a source was made and what happened; who it addresses; why it was produced and possible motives; how the creator’s position shapes its message; and how it supports, corroborates or challenges an argument and connects to outside information. Support sourcing claims with evidence. The missing two documents and Mongols homework are excluded.

terms.Sahel: Transition between Sahara and savanna; from Arabic for shores.
terms.Caravan: People traveling together for protection, trade or pilgrimage.
terms.Caravanserai: Roadside inn or caravan stopping place, also a trading center.
terms.Pastoralist: Person whose livelihood involves herding animals.
terms.Madrasa: A school associated with Islamic learning in the passages.
terms.Cosmopolitan: Containing communities and influences from many regions.
terms.Historical Ghana: The West African kingdom shown in the class material, distinct from modern Ghana.
terms.Sourcing: Evaluating context, audience, purpose and viewpoint before using evidence.
